title: Micro-transfer-printed DRAM tiles onto logic replace TSV stacking
idea: Extreme user: flexible wearables built by elastomer-stamp transfer printing. Release thin DRAM tiles by undercutting a sacrificial layer, pick thousands at once with a PDMS stamp and print them face-up onto logic wafers, then connect them with a thin-film redistribution layer.
why: HBM TSV tax: no TSVs or micro-bumps and wafer-scale parallel placement; recovers much of HBM's ~3x area penalty and 20-30% yield loss.

title: Anamartic's wafer-scale memory returns as uncut DRAM wafer blades
idea: Anamartic's 'Catt spiral' wafer-scale memory shipped in 1989 but died on weak 1980s yields and cheap boards. Today's dies carry redundancy, so skip dicing, known-good-die test and packaging: one redistribution layer daisy-chains good dies via a self-configuring spiral bus mapped at wafer test, and whole 300 mm wafers (~2 TB) mount as AI-rack memory blades.
why: Removes dicing, packaging, substrates and per-die final test (~10-20% of DRAM cost) and sidesteps the advanced-packaging capacity bottleneck.

title: Tumbling bricks: fluidic self-assembly of DRAM micro-tiles onto logic
idea: Fabricate 200 um trapezoidal DRAM array tiles at one high-yield site, then tumble them in a carrier liquid over logic wafers with matching etched recesses (RFID fluidic assembly style) so shape keys and capillary/solder forces seat each tile, followed by batch bonding and one redistribution layer.
why: Capital/Fact 6: parallel placement of millions of known-good tiles per hour, no TSV stacks or interposers; memory sits on logic like cache.

title: Unsawn wafer as memory module: no dicing, packaging or DIMMs
idea: Constraint: zero back-end line. Ship the whole 300 mm DRAM wafer as a ~1.5 TB memory slab: a wafer-level redistribution layer stitches good dies into a mesh, bad dies are fenced off, edge SerDes expose CXL ports and a cold plate bonds to the back.
why: Test, packaging and module assembly are ~15-25% of DRAM cost; removing them while using every good die gives ~20% lower cost per bit and a rack-scale product.

title: Chef's mise en place: bank generic array wafers, personalize later
idea: Chefs prep ingredients before the orders arrive. Build one standard cell-array-only wafer (capacitors, access transistors, bitlines, no periphery) in huge volume on a stripped-down array fab, stockpile it, then hybrid-bond it to a periphery wafer made in any CMOS foundry, choosing a DDR5, LPDDR or HBM-base personality at bonding time.
why: The array fab needs ~1/3 fewer tool types and no high-performance periphery transistors; the periphery (~49% of die, fact 7) moves to cheaper logic capacity; the wafer bank absorbs demand swings. Risks: ~1 um bond pitch per sense-amp group, and paying for two wafers.

title: Knitting: loop-end wordline layout deletes the SAQP cut mask
idea: Random stimulus 'knitting' (one yarn, closed loops, nothing cut) -> instead of cutting the closed ends of self-aligned quadruple-patterned spacer loops, which takes an extra critical mask, each loop is used as ONE electrical wordline that crosses two transistor rows. The active-area pattern is staggered so that each bitline contact sees only one gate in the loop, and the loop ends land on a sacrificial 'selvedge' strip that a blanket CMP trims away.
why: Removes 1-2 critical cut exposures, often EUV or double-patterned ArFi, per array layer, saving ~3-6% of wafer cost. Paired drive also halves the number of wordline drivers, which shrinks periphery (fact 7).

title: Delete retention-tail implants and anneals; codes absorb the leakers
idea: Combine the cell recipe with system coding: the halo and compensation implant masks and the extended hydrogen anneal, which exist only to tame the 13 fA leakage tail, are removed. The ~1% of cells that then fall below 64 ms retention are absorbed by scrub plus code.
why: Drops ~2-3 implant masks and a long furnace step (~3% wafer cost) and the multi-hour hot retention-screen test (fact 3).

title: Egg-grading economics: retention-graded dies sold with refresh maps
idea: Food grading sells every egg by grade; test each DRAM die's retention tail and sell weaker dies as a managed-refresh grade with a per-die weak-row map stored on the module, so the controller refreshes only those rows faster instead of the die being repaired or scrapped.
why: Effective fab output: recovers ~5-10% of dies lost to retention fails or repair limits and needs fewer redundant rows and fuses (fact 7); each yield point is ~1% cost per bit.

title: Spin-coated, UV-cured indium-zinc oxide access transistors in BEOL
idea: Box: MIM charge x solution-processed InZnO TFT x voltage sense amp x BEOL x Si or glass x sol-gel spin coating plus deep-UV photo-annealing below 250 C. A nitrate precursor coats the topography and 185/254 nm UV generates ozone and radicals that condense the oxide network, reaching 5-20 cm2/Vs with no vacuum deposition.
why: Removes sputter/ALD clusters from the access-device module (capital); uses only a spin coater and UV lamp; risk is trap density widening the leakage tail and thickness control in 3D topography.

title: Certified pre-owned DRAM: re-profiled hyperscaler memory with warranty
idea: Borrowed from certified pre-owned cars: a 10-person shop buys DIMMs from retired cloud servers by the ton, runs 48-hour retention, row-hammer and temperature profiling on FPGA test rigs, rewrites each DIMM's SPD with measured timing and refresh bins, swaps weak chips and sells warrantied modules for CXL memory expanders.
why: Supply: millions of DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs retire yearly; reuse adds supply with zero wafer capacity at ~30-50% of new price.

title: Fab in reverse: harvest DRAM dies from retired servers
idea: Po: the fab runs backwards. Industrialize de-population of retired server DIMMs and boards: desolder packages, re-ball, test and rebin them into CXL memory expanders for tier-2 workloads, with a controller that tolerates mixed speed grades.
why: Capital intensity: ~1/100 of new-fab capex per GB; hyperscalers retire tens of petabytes per year, a few percent of global bit supply available within months.

title: Passive RF resonators let every wafer report its own metrology
idea: Ideal: zero metrology tools. Closest: scribe lines carry passive LC resonators built from the layers made so far, whose resonance shifts with CD, film thickness and overlay; a contactless RF reader in each load port interrogates every wafer in seconds after each module, replacing sampled CD-SEM/OCD for go/no-go.
why: Fact 4: metrology/inspection is ~10-15% of fab capex and adds cycle time; 100% wafer coverage catches excursions days earlier and raises yield.

title: Kovio's liquid-silicon ink printed into 32 cheap gain-cell tiers
idea: Kovio printed silicon RFID from liquid cyclopentasilane and folded in 2014 on a tiny market and hard-to-handle pyrophoric ink. Inside a sealed inert coater module, spin 20 nm silicon films from ink, crystallize only the top film with a nanosecond laser, and stack 32 tiers of poly-Si 2T gain cells, each tier patterned by one imprint.
why: Meets 100x: each tier costs a spin, a laser scan and one imprint (~$5-10/wafer) instead of epitaxy or transfer; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: grain-boundary leakage forces ms refresh and defect mapping.

title: Gutenberg's fixed type: a single-pattern scanner that prints only arrays
idea: A printer would not buy a universal press to print one page forever. Build a stripped-down ArF or EUV exposure tool with a hard-mounted periodic array mask (no reticle handler or library, fixed dipole illumination, smaller fixed-field optics) that only steps the array pattern die to die, leaving periphery to flexible scanners.
why: Dropping reticle-stage dynamics, pupil flexibility and reticle logistics could cut tool price ~50-70% and raise array-layer throughput ~30%, and is easier for a second supplier to build. Risk: an EUV version still needs the EUV source.

title: Mitochondrial cristae ribs fold lateral capacitors into short 3D cells
idea: Cristae multiply membrane area by inward folds; build each lateral capacitor tier from a mini-superlattice of three SiGe sub-layers with different Ge content, so the single lateral wet recess carves a rib-and-groove cavity and the electrode/dielectric deposited into it gains ~3x area per unit length.
why: Each capacitor leaf can be ~3x shorter for the same Cs (fact 1), shrinking cell pitch in every tier; a 40-tier stack then reaches ~10x planar bits/mm2 at near-flat cost because the ribs come from deposition, not lithography.

title: MLCC laminate: interdigitated plates replace the tall pillar capacitor
idea: Copy multilayer-ceramic-capacitor stacking: deposit ~30 alternating TiN and Ru electrode layers separated by 5 nm high-k into a 300 nm stack, cut per-cell blocks, then selectively recess Ru on one sidewall and TiN on the other with different wet chemistries so each wall contacts only odd or only even plates.
why: Fact 1: ~5 fF from a 300 nm stack at AR ~15 (vs 1.5 um at 70:1) on a relaxed non-EUV ~20 nm cell; removes the hardest etch.

title: Wafer vendor ships memory substrates with buried back-gate planes
idea: Ideal: the memory maker buys a wafer that is already half a memory. Closest: a bonded Smart-Cut substrate with a buried n+ back-gate plane under thin BOX and a 10 nm Si film; the fab runs a plain planar logic flow and gets double-gate floating-body 1T cells whose negative back-gate holds stored holes, with no capacitor.
why: Facts 1, 4, 7: removes ~25-30% of DRAM front-end steps and shifts that work to cheap substrate-bonding lines; lets FD-SOI-style logic fabs make 1T memory.

title: Anodic alumina self-ordered pores as the capacitor mold
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of plasma-etching 70:1 holes, grow them - deposit ~1.5 um aluminium over the array, nano-indent or DUV-print a shallow pit lattice at the storage-node pitch, and anodize so pores self-propagate straight down at 100:1+; widen pores, open the barrier oxide, then ALD the electrode and dielectric.
why: Replaces the costliest HAR etch (high-power/cryo RIE, many chamber-hours) with a room-temperature electrochemical bath at <1% of the capex; aspect ratio becomes nearly free, so Cs can rise toward 8-10 fF (facts 1, 4).

title: Catalyst-grown vertical nanowire forests replace etched capacitor pillars
idea: Ideal: capacitor pillars that build themselves upward. Closest: DSA-placed catalyst dots on each storage contact seed vertical vapor-liquid-solid growth of doped-Si nanowires to 1-1.5 um; TiN, high-k and top plate are ALD-wrapped around them, so there is no mold, HAR etch or wet dip-out.
why: Facts 1 and 4: AR set by growth time, not etch physics; removes mold deposition, HAR etch and collapse-prone drying; capacitor module step count roughly halved.

title: Perfect-binding spine: print stack interconnect on the die edges
idea: Stack thinned DRAM dies like book signatures with all inter-die wiring routed to one polished edge, then pattern vertical interconnect along that spine by laser-direct-write seeding and electroplating, the way a binder glues a spine, eliminating TSVs and their keep-out zones.
why: Fact 6: removes the TSV area/yield tax (~3x area per bit, -20-30% yield) and TSV etch/fill/reveal tools; a ~10 um spine pitch still gives thousands of channels per edge.

title: Coaxial gallium-oxide 2T0C cell grown inside one vertical hole
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: in a 3D-NAND-like stack of word planes, one DUV-printed hole receives nested ALD shells at each tier recess - an outer amorphous Ga2O3 write channel gated by the plane, a metal storage-node ring, a thin dielectric, and an inner Ga2O3 read channel gated by that ring.
why: Ga2O3's 4.8 eV gap gives off-current below ~1e-21 A, so retention exceeds years and refresh is zero with no capacitor module; one hole mask serves 32-64 tiers, raising density without EUV (facts 2, 3, 4).

title: Precious-metal streaming finance for DRAM wafer starts
idea: Borrowed from royalty-streaming firms like Franco-Nevada, which fund mines upfront for a fixed share of future metal at a fixed low price with a small staff: a 10-person fund pays ~20% of a DRAM line's capex in exchange for 10% of its wafer output for 15 years at cash cost, and resells the bits on long-term contracts to hyperscalers.
why: Capital intensity: non-dilutive, non-debt capex lowers the cost of capital for new fabs and gives buyers a hedge against 4x price spikes.

title: Aircraft-leasing model for EUV and high-NA scanners
idea: Borrowed from aviation, where lessors like AerCap own about half of airline jets and redeploy them: a scanner lessor owns EUV tools, leases them per wafer pass to memory makers, moves tools between fabs as cycles shift, and funds itself with asset-backed securities on scanner residual value.
why: Fact 4: depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost; turning $200M+ tool capex into opex lowers entry cost for new or U.S. DRAM fabs and damps the boom-bust cycle.

title: Repurpose overbuilt US SiC power fabs for refresh-free SiC DRAM
idea: Extreme user: 200C automotive and downhole electronics. 4H-SiC's 3.2 eV bandgap gives ~10^-20 A off-current, so a small planar capacitor retains for hours; build relaxed-density refresh-free memory for industrial/auto on the 150-200 mm SiC lines now underused as EV demand slowed.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: uses existing domestic SiC capacity; removes refresh and the capacitor etch module for the industrial/auto segment.

title: Core-rope weights: maskless via-programmed BEOL ROM frees HBM
idea: Revive Apollo's core-rope memory, where the wiring itself encoded the program: build generic base wafers with 8 stacked metal crossbar levels and encode a frozen model's weights only in the via layers, written maskless by multibeam e-beam, so each model ships as a ROM chiplet. Weights leave DRAM; HBM keeps only activations and KV cache.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: static weights are ~50-80% of inference memory; 4F2 per via level x 8 levels at 40 nm metal pitch is ~DRAM-class density with no capacitor, no refresh and no per-model mask set.

title: Electrorefine wafering kerf back into crystal feedstock
idea: First principle: diamond-wire slicing turns ~100-150 um of 11N Si per cut into sludge, yet the Si atoms are still pure. Collect the kerf, separate abrasive and coolant, strip the surface oxide, and electrorefine and remelt it into polysilicon feedstock for the next boule.
why: Scarce resource and polysilicon cost: recovers ~15-25% of crystal mass now lost per wafer; recycled by design.

title: Home-built atmospheric spatial ALD deposits capacitor high-k without vacuum
idea: Effect: self-limiting chemisorption separated in space. A gas-bearing head keeps precursor and oxidant zones apart with N2 curtains, so the ALD half-reactions happen as the wafer moves under it at atmospheric pressure, depositing ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 at ~10x the rate of temporal ALD. $1M funds two heads, precursors and 24 months of electrical tests on capacitor molds.
why: Capital: vacuum ALD tools cost $3-5M; an atmospheric tool at ~$300k with higher throughput cuts deposition cost of ownership. Conformality in HAR holes is the risk.

title: 77 K memory tier lets fabs drop recessed-gate access transistors
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter changes: run memory racks in liquid-nitrogen immersion, where thermally activated junction and subthreshold leakage fall by >20 orders of magnitude and only tunneling remains, so low-field planar cells hold charge effectively indefinitely while cold and refresh is switched off; the fab then builds simple planar or shallow-fin access transistors instead of the 3-4 mask buried-channel module.
why: Zero refresh power; ~8-10% fewer process steps and relaxed gate-layer patterning, plus higher mobility at 77 K; the ~10 W-wall-per-W cooling overhead is offset by removing refresh and leakage and denser racks (facts 3, 4).

title: Substitute bulk silicon with back-gated FD-SOI for dynamic-threshold cells
idea: Build the array on ultra-thin-body SOI with a buried back-gate plane held at deep negative bias during retention (high Vt, low leakage) and pulsed toward zero only under the activated mat, so the front wordline needs only a ~0.8 V swing; the recessed-channel BCAT etch module and VPP pumps go away.
why: Constraint: wordline energy ~14x lower (0.8 V vs 3 V) and lower bitline voltage give ~8-12x per access; facet: deletes the recessed-gate litho/etch module.

title: Glassmaker's float line: continuous linear fab instead of cluster tools
idea: Pilkington made glass as a continuous floating ribbon instead of cast sheets. Build the DRAM front end as a linear tunnel where wafers move nose-to-tail on carriers through in-line deposition, etch and clean stations (spatial-ALD heads, linear plasma sources) set by takt time, with litho as the only off-line island, so in-line segments have no FOUPs, stockers or overhead hoists.
why: Cuts AMHS, buffers and floor space (~15-20% of fab cost) and cycle time from ~90 to ~40 days; in-line stations run near 100% utilization, so fewer tools are needed. Risks: one station stalls the line (needs bypass loops), and recipe flexibility.

title: Relax F to 38 nm, magnify tiers to 300
idea: Minify lithography demand by freezing lateral pitch at a DUV-immersion 38 nm and magnify vertical tiers to 300 using NAND-style alternating deposition, one hole etch per 50 tiers, and a vertical-channel gain cell, so deposition and etch replace EUV.
why: Litho-bound scaling and EUV dependence: zero EUV layers; density grows with deposition tools costing ~1/4 of an EUV scanner per wafer-pass, targeting >2x bits per wafer at lower capex per bit.

title: Toaster: millisecond flash-lamp anneals stack 32 ferroelectric tiers monolithically
idea: Random stimulus 'pop-up toaster' (brief surface heat) -> each newly deposited HZO tier is crystallized by a 1-20 ms xenon flash or laser that heats only the top ~100 nm to >600 C while buried tiers and CMOS stay <400 C. This enables monolithic 32-tier FeRAM/FeFET stacking in BEOL.
why: Non-volatile 3D memory without wafer bonding. Density per litho area scales with tier count, and wafer cost per bit falls ~5-10x at 32 tiers.

title: Lighthouse: one free-electron-laser EUV source shared by many scanners
idea: Random stimulus 'lighthouse' (one beam serves many ships) -> a U.S.-built energy-recovery-linac free-electron laser produces ~10 kW of EUV and splits it among 10-20 scanner bodies, replacing per-scanner tin-plasma sources with their CO2 drive lasers.
why: EUV single-supplier and cost (fact 4): source power and uptime limit EUV throughput. A shared FEL could double wafers per hour and cut EUV cost per layer ~40%, and it creates U.S. ownership of the source.

title: One accelerator-driven EUV light source feeds a dozen scanners
idea: Po: the scanner has no light of its own. A free-electron laser producing ~10 kW at 13.5 nm distributes light by beamlines to 10-20 scanner bodies, replacing a tin-droplet plasma source in every tool.
why: EUV cost and power: source is a big share of scanner cost and nearly all its energy; ~2-3x lower cost per EUV layer and far less power per wafer.

title: Nanoimprint-only array layers, DUV periphery: EUV-free 1T1C DRAM
idea: Box: Si-capacitor charge x buried-channel access x voltage sense amp x 2D monolithic x 300 mm Si x jet-and-flash nanoimprint. The strictly periodic array layers (active, buried WL, BL, storage-node contact, capacitor holes) are imprinted from e-beam-written masters into jetted resist, while the irregular, relaxed-pitch periphery stays on DUV immersion; overlay is held by a magnification-actuated template chuck and in-situ moire alignment marks.
why: Litho-bound capital (fact 4): replaces 5-7 EUV layers with imprint tools at roughly 1/4-1/5 of EUV capex and ~90% less litho energy; claims 20-30% lower wafer cost if imprint defectivity reaches <0.1/cm2.

title: Multibeam e-beam direct write replaces masks for irregular layers
idea: Po: masks don't exist. Use a ~250k-beam electron writer (today's mask-writer technology) directly on wafers for the irregular, low-area layers (periphery cuts, fuse/redundancy personalization, product variants) while periodic array layers use cheap patterning.
why: Mask cost and EUV dependence: removes $10M+ mask sets per product spin and EUV for irregular layers; product variants in days.

title: Domestic multi-column e-beam writes periphery and cut layers maskless
idea: Use thousands of parallel miniature e-beam columns built in the U.S. to direct-write only the sparse, irregular layers (periphery contacts, cut masks, chip IDs), while self-assembly or imprint handles the dense arrays.
why: Eliminates ~10-15 masks per product ($10-20M per node) and imported scanners on those layers; product variants turn in days.

title: Pottery bisque-then-glaze: capacitor-first flow, transistors on transferred silicon
idea: Borrowed from pottery, where the clay body is fired hot first and the glaze cooler later: build the capacitor array first with a 700-800 C crystallized SrTiO3 or rutile TiO2 dielectric (k~100), planarize, Smart-Cut-transfer a thin single-crystal Si film on top, then form access transistors at <=450 C with laser dopant activation.
why: Fact 1: unlocks k~100 dielectrics that need temperatures transistors cannot survive, so AR can drop from ~70 to ~35 for the same Cs, roughly halving capacitor etch cost and tool count.

title: Maskless multi-beam writing for periphery, mask-defined SAQP for array
idea: Combine 260k-beamlet e-beam writers, today used only to make masks, with the DRAM product flow. Irregular, sparse periphery layers that change with every product are direct-written with no reticle, while the regular array uses one shared immersion-SAQP mask set.
why: Removes ~10-15 periphery reticles per product (a $10-20M mask set per design spin). LPDDR, HBM-core and custom AI SKUs can share one array mask set, which lowers the capital barrier for new U.S. entrants.

title: Grow up, not shrink down: relaxed-pitch 3D DRAM at F~38 nm
idea: Reverse the scaling vector: freeze lateral pitch where single ArF immersion exposure works (F~38 nm) and get density from 48-64 monolithic tiers whose shared vertical wordline is patterned once per stack, not once per tier.
why: No EUV; litho cost per bit falls with tier count; at 48 tiers density ~5x today's 2D at ~1/3 litho cost.

title: C: closed-loop supercritical CO2 removes post-etch residues
idea: Replace aqueous/semi-aqueous post-etch residue removal and its DI rinse with supercritical CO2 carrying a few percent chelating co-solvent in a pressure cell; the CO2 is recompressed and recycled >95%.
why: Water: post-etch cleans recur dozens of times per DRAM flow, and their water drops >10x; zero surface tension also protects high-AR pillars and 3D tiers.

title: Steel mini-mill disruption: EUV-free DUV mini-fabs for mature DRAM
idea: Nucor beat integrated mills by entering at rebar with cheap electric-arc mini-mills; build 10-20k wafer-starts/month fabs using refurbished 193i scanners and SAQP to make 1y/1z-class DDR4, LPDDR4 and CXL-expander dies, sell into the commodity tier the HBM-focused majors are abandoning, then climb node by node.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: ~$3-5B per mini-fab versus $15B+; zero EUV; DUV tools are available on the secondary market; adds supply in under 3 years.

title: Morpho-wing interference lithography prints the periodic cell array maskless
idea: Morpho scales make color by multilayer interference; the DRAM array is a perfect lattice, so expose active, buried-wordline and storage-node layers with 3- or 6-beam 193 nm immersion interference (~70 nm pitch hexagonal lattice, near-zero roughness), then one spacer doubling to ~35 nm. Array edges are trimmed and periphery printed afterwards with a cheap ArF mask.
why: Moves 3-4 of the 5-7 EUV array exposures onto a laser-and-optics bench costing ~1/20 of an EUV scanner (fact 4); est. 15-20% lower wafer cost and a large capex cut.

title: Chromatophore-shrink mastering makes nanoimprint templates without e-beam writers
idea: Squid chromatophores expand and contract pigment sacs elastically; write nanoimprint master patterns at 4x size with cheap i-line lithography on a resist atop a biaxially pre-stretched shape-memory polymer, release it so the relief shrinks 4x, then electroform a nickel or replicate a quartz daughter. Shrink distortion is measured once and pre-compensated in the 4x layout.
why: E-beam NIL mastering costs ~$0.5-1M and weeks per layer; this targets <$20k and days, making nanoimprint viable for DRAM layers that now need EUV (fact 4).

title: Display-fab DRAM: oxide 1T1C arrays on Gen-8.5 glass panels
idea: Borrowed from LCD/OLED backplane fabs: run IGZO 1T1C memory tiles on idle Gen-8.5 (2.2x2.5 m) glass lines, which pattern ~1-1.5 um features with cheap panel steppers at a few $/cm2, deposit 4-8 oxide tiers per panel, then dice into tiles flip-bonded over a small CMOS periphery die.
why: Capital intensity and idle-capacity reuse: depreciated display fabs cost ~50x less per processed cm2 than 300 mm DRAM lines; density is 10x+ worse per tier, so it only pays as a slow bulk tier or with many stacked tiers.

title: Shrinky Dinks lithography: pattern large, heat-shrink into imprint masters
idea: Borrowed from the Shrinky Dinks toy, whose pre-stretched polystyrene shrinks ~2.5x when baked: write DRAM array master patterns oversized on pre-stretched shape-memory polymer with cheap optical lithography, shrink thermally, electroform a hard nickel copy as a NIL master, and repeat for a second shrink stage, all in a garage-scale lab.
why: Fact 4: master fabrication without e-beam or EUV; edge roughness and non-uniform shrink below 50 nm make it speculative.

title: Child's Shrinky Dinks: implosion-fabricated nanoimprint master templates
idea: A child shrinks drawings in the oven. Write the template pattern at 10x scale with a cheap laser into an expanded hydrogel, deposit metal or oxide into the written voxels, then dehydrate so the gel shrinks ~10x isotropically to sub-20 nm features, and use the shrunken part as a master for nanoimprint templates.
why: Replaces days of $10M+ e-beam master writing with cheap optics; template cost and turnaround fall ~10x, supporting imprint-based array patterning. Speculative: distortion over cm-scale fields, and edge fidelity.

title: Multi-beam e-beam writes only cuts, making DRAM variants maskless
idea: Constraint: no new mask set per product. Print array gratings once with cheap periodic litho, then use a ~250k-beam electron writer only on sparse cut and via layers (<5% exposed area) to customize die size, ECC layout and bank count.
why: Mask sets cost $10-20M; cut-only exposure makes e-beam throughput viable (~10-20 wph) for specialty and low-volume DRAM lines.

title: Substitute EUV projection optics with X-ray proximity printing from storage rings
idea: A compact electron storage ring feeds 12-16 soft-X-ray (~1 nm) beamlines, each exposing wafers through a 1x membrane mask held 5-10 um away; there are no mirrors to build, and the dense periodic array tolerates 1x masks written by e-beam.
why: Fact 4: ends single-supplier EUV dependence; source capital is shared across many steppers, possibly 2-3x lower cost per array layer. 1x mask distortion and cost are the risks.

title: Refurbished tools fill empty shells of existing fab sites
idea: Po: factories build factories. Buy decommissioned 193i scanners, etchers and ALD tools from closing 200/300 mm lines, refurbish them and install them into unused cleanroom shell space already built at existing DRAM and logic sites.
why: Capital and time: shell and utilities (~30% of fab cost, 2+ years) are already sunk; trailing capacity online in ~12 months at ~25-35% of greenfield cost.

title: Deep-trench storage revival from America's eDRAM heritage
idea: Revive the substrate deep-trench capacitor of the IBM/New York eDRAM lineage for standalone DRAM: trenches etched ~10 um into silicon beneath the transistor hold ~20 fF, freeing the surface for an 8F2 cell built on existing U.S. logic-fab trench tooling.
why: Escapes the stacked-capacitor AR wall (Fact 1) with charge to spare, allowing 4x longer retention (Fact 3) and no high-AR stack module, at some density cost.

title: TV maker's view: DRAM gain-cell tiles on idle Gen-10.5 display lines
idea: A display engineer notes that LCD/OLED fabs already process 9 m2 glass at <=350 C with oxide-TFT tools, and many sit idle. Add panel-scale nanoimprint for ~100 nm features, build 2T0C oxide-semiconductor gain-cell arrays at <=350 C on Gen-10.5 glass, and cut them into memory tiles for CXL far memory, attaching periphery chiplets.
why: At F=100 nm and 8F2, one panel holds ~15 TB of raw cells, with capex per m2 ~50-100x below a wafer fab: a possible <$1/GB capacity tier. High risk: imprint overlay on large glass with thermal expansion, and speed of long panel wires.

title: Pollen-tube confined epitaxy grows monocrystalline channels in every tier
idea: A pollen tube grows only inside the style's channel; deposit a cheap 120-pair PECVD oxide/nitride stack as in 3D NAND, strip the nitride through slits to leave tunnels, then grow single-crystal Si into all tunnels at once by template-confined lateral epitaxy seeded from the substrate at each slit base.
why: Replaces slow, strain-limited Si/SiGe epitaxial superlattices (capped near 30-60 layers) with 3D-NAND-cost stacks, making 120 tiers (~10x bits/mm2) affordable at near-flat wafer cost (fact 2).

title: Mars-colony do-everything single chamber for regional DRAM minifabs
idea: Extreme user: a Mars colony that can land one tool, not 400. A reconfigurable plasma chamber with swappable gas manifolds and an in-situ ALD head runs etch, deposition, clean and anneal sequentially on one wafer; a minifab of 30 such chambers plus one scanner trades throughput for a 10x smaller tool count.
why: Capital/time: regional DRAM capacity for ~$1-2B and 12-18 months instead of $15B and 4 years; good for trusted/defense volume and fast ramp.

title: CVD diamond substrates remove the thermal ceiling on stacking
idea: Worse: stack memory on a substrate that traps heat, so retention collapses and refresh doubles above 85 C. Flip: build tiers on thin polycrystalline CVD diamond plates (~1500 W/mK) that hold stacked arrays near coolant temperature. Leakage roughly halves for each ~10 C of cooling, so stacks of 16-24 tiers stay viable.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and HBM thermals: ~2-4x retention and more tiers per stack; diamond is grown from methane in U.S. reactors.

title: GE's BEAMOS reborn: microcolumn electron beams address unpatterned MOS film
idea: GE's 1970s beam-addressed MOS memory (BEAMOS) wrote and read charge on a MOS target with an electron beam, but died on bulky vacuum tubes and slow deflection. Wafer-fabricate 10,000 MEMS microcolumns in a chip-scale vacuum package, each deflecting a 10-20 nm spot across a 100 um field of an unpatterned SiO2/Si target and reading bits by beam-induced current.
why: Meets 100x: the storage medium needs zero lithography and each column covers ~25 Mb; est. $0.02-0.1/GB. Trades: vacuum packaging, ~100 ns-1 us access, beam-induced oxide wear limits endurance unless run at low voltage.

title: Two-slot piggy bank: finance NV-memory fabs from memory plus storage budgets
idea: Random stimulus 'piggy bank with two slots' -> because the product is non-volatile, it is sold to hyperscalers as both the DRAM tier and a hot-storage/write-cache tier. Take-or-pay prepurchase agreements from both budgets are pooled into securitized fab financing.
why: Capital intensity: drawing on two procurement budgets doubles the addressable spend that backs one fab, lowers the cost of capital, and makes a $5-8B U.S. NV-memory fab financeable years sooner.

title: Rotary spatial ALD conveyor for capacitor dielectric stacks
idea: Worse: deposit ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 capacitor stacks by slow pulse-purge temporal ALD. Flip: carry wafers on a rotating platen under gas-curtain-separated precursor zones (spatial ALD from solar passivation), so each revolution is one cycle at ~10x throughput and higher precursor utilization.
why: Throughput/capital: capacitor dielectric/electrode tool count falls ~60-80% and Zr/Hf precursor use drops.

title: Plywood DRAM: laser-lifted polyimide tiers laminated into stacks
idea: Worse: grow 26+ tiers sequentially on one substrate, so one bad tier scraps them all. Flip: fabricate each tier in parallel on polyimide over a reusable glass carrier, test it, laser-lift-off the good ones with OLED LLO tools, and laminate 32 known-good tiers with self-aligned through-tier vias.
why: 3D DRAM (fact 2): known-good-tier stacking breaks the compounded-yield trap and reuses idle OLED tools.

title: Substitute lithographic critical dimensions with sidewall-deposited film thicknesses
idea: Lay the cell on its side: gate length, channel thickness and capacitor dielectric are all set by ALD film thickness on sidewalls of coarse DUV-defined steps, so atomic-precision deposition replaces nm-precision lithography. Each tier needs only one coarse block mask because F no longer sets channel length.
why: Fact 4: breaks litho-bound scaling, since feature size follows ALD (+/-0.1 nm) instead of EUV; could remove 4-5 EUV layers per wafer.

title: Apical-meristem nanowires grow stacked transistors along their own axis
idea: Shoots add segments at the tip; grow vertical Si nanowires by catalyst-tip (VLS) growth from the pad lattice while switching dopant and Ge gases every ~25 nm, so each wire holds 16 axial n+/p/n+ transistor segments, then fill around the forest with alternating spin-on dielectric and conductor layers that become wordline tiers timed to the segments.
why: Channels for all 16 tiers come from one growth run instead of patterning; at ~40 nm wire pitch that is ~100 nm2 per bit, ~8-10x bits/mm2 at roughly flat cost (fact 2).

title: MRI zero-boil-off approach: helium recapture skids for fab tools
idea: Borrowed from modern MRI magnets, which lose almost no helium because a cryocooler recondenses boil-off: a small team builds bolt-on skids that collect helium from chuck backside, leak-check and purge exhausts, run it through a membrane separator, pressure-swing adsorber and cryo-purifier, and return 6N helium to the tool manifold.
why: Scarce resource: recapturing 70-90% of fab helium shields DRAM output from the Qatar outage for roughly $1M per fab.

title: Oblique ion-sputter ripples self-organize sub-pitch word-line gratings
idea: Effect: Bradley-Harper sputter instability. 500 eV Ar+ ions hitting a hardmask 60-70 degrees off normal grow ripples with a 20-30 nm period on their own, and a coarse ArF pre-pattern at 4x that period pins the ripple phase and direction (guided self-organization). The ripples are transferred as the word-line grating, replacing SAQP's spacer deposition and etch loops with one broad-beam step.
why: Fact 4: SAQP takes ~12-16 steps per layer; one broad-beam ion step could cut that layer's cost ~60% with no EUV. Ripple defectivity is the open risk.

title: Rayleigh-Plateau breakup converts one line pattern into dot arrays
idea: Effect: Rayleigh-Plateau capillary instability. Print a single 1D grating of thin amorphous-Si or Cu lines, then anneal: each line breaks into droplets at a fixed wavelength (~4.5x the line diameter), and shallow notches printed by the same mask pin the droplet positions. One litho step yields a 2D landing-pad or node array instead of two crossed patterning passes.
why: Fact 4: honeycomb pad and node layers use crossed double or quad patterning; merging the two passes saves an EUV or SAQP pass per layer, ~10-15% of array litho cost.

title: Pasta extruder: drawn nanochannel glass bonded as capacitor mold
idea: Random stimulus 'pasta extruder' -> a glass preform with ordered core rods is drawn, stacked and redrawn several times, as microchannel plates are made, down to ~30 nm channels. Wafer-thin slices are bonded onto the transistor wafer, and the cores are etched out to leave AR >100 capacitor molds.
why: Capacitor charge wall and capital (facts 1 and 4): ~10^11 channels/cm2 are made by fiber drawing with zero litho, and the mold step moves out of the fab into a glass plant.

title: Ti: oxidize the TiN electrode into its own rutile dielectric
idea: Instead of ALD-depositing ZrO2 and then a top electrode, convert the outer 4-6 nm of the TiN bottom electrode into rutile TiO2 (k~80-100) with an ozone/radical oxidation that co-incorporates Al from a pre-dosed monolayer to suppress leakage; one conversion step replaces hundreds of ALD cycles and is conformal at any AR.
why: Fact 1 (k~70 needed) plus throughput: deletes the longest ALD tool-time step of the capacitor module; conversion is self-conformal so deeper holes cost no extra time. Leakage of TiO2 is the open risk.

title: Zuse relay storage reborn as bistable buckled-nanobeam memory
idea: Revive the relay storage of Konrad Zuse's 1941 Z3, which held its memory in ~1,400 latching relays, as pre-buckled nanobeams with two stable shapes that snap between states under an electrostatic pulse and are read capacitively without ever touching a contact. Beams are released with vapour HF and sealed in vacuum, so the cell's off state is an empty gap.
why: Fact 3 under the constraint: mechanical bistability has no leakage tail and needs no refresh, and non-contact snapping avoids wear; ~4 BEOL masks with no rare gas, ~10 ns switching. Risks are cell size (~20-30F2) and beam fatigue at 1e15+ cycles.

title: Hydrogen-anneal surface migration forms stacked silicon-on-nothing tiers for 3D DRAM
idea: Effect: surface-energy-driven Si migration in H2. Etch a lattice of deep holes with periodic diameter modulation (scallops), then anneal in H2 at ~1100 C: surface diffusion closes each scallop into a flat buried void, giving several single-crystal Si sheets separated by empty plates (multi-layer silicon-on-nothing). Filling the voids with oxide yields 3D DRAM tiers without a 100+ layer Si/SiGe epitaxial superlattice.
why: Fact 2: the epi superlattice is the costliest and most defect-prone 3D DRAM module; an etch plus anneal could save ~$300-600 per wafer and remove strain-warpage limits on tier count.

title: Sea sponge chemistry: catalytic room-temperature silica gap fill
idea: Sea sponges build glass spicules at 10 C with silicatein enzymes. Tether biomimetic amine or peptide catalysts to trench walls so they polymerize silica (or titania) bottom-up from aqueous precursors at room temperature, filling isolation and inter-tier gaps without voids, then densify at <=400 C.
why: Replaces HDP-CVD and spin-on glass that need ~1000 C densification, along with their tools; bottom-up growth fills AR >20 gaps where CVD leaves voids. High risk: film density, moisture, breakdown field.

title: Panel-scale nanoimprinted oxide gain cells on depreciated display lines
idea: Jump from a 0.07 m2 wafer to 5.5 m2 Gen-8.5 display mother-glass: retired LCD/OLED lines run panel-scale nanoimprint at ~50 nm half-pitch to build 8 stacked low-temperature oxide-semiconductor 2T0C gain-cell tiers, which are diced into memory tiles and bonded to silicon periphery chiplets.
why: Capital intensity: display fabs are fully depreciated and processed area costs ~50-100x less per m2 than a DRAM wafer, so ~8 tiers at 50 nm can reach cost-per-bit parity for a capacity tier without new fab capex.

title: Display-industry sputtered zinc oxynitride channels for back-end gain-cell tiers
idea: The display industry sputters large-area oxide TFT channels; with In and Ga banned, use reactive-sputtered zinc oxynitride (ZnON, mobility ~50-100 cm2/Vs) with Al2O3/SiO2 gates to stack 2T0C gain-cell tiers above CMOS, each tier made by room-temperature sputtering and DUV litho, no epitaxy.
why: 3D DRAM manufacturability (fact 2) and capex (fact 4): tiers come from cheap PVD tools; Zn, O, N, Al are abundant. Risk: ZnON stability and leakage tail.

title: Eliminate leading-edge logic for HBM base dies: depreciated 28 nm US fabs
idea: Make HBM3E/HBM4-compatible base dies in fully depreciated 28-40 nm US logic fabs, using wider, slower internal channels to the core dies and a 28 nm PHY tuned to the JEDEC data rate. The GPU sees a standard HBM stack.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: avoids competing for scarce 5/3 nm wafers; base-die wafer cost falls ~5-10x with near-zero depreciation.

title: 5 mm2 DRAM dielets tolerate dirtier fabs via exponential yield
idea: Shrink the die from ~70 mm2 to ~5 mm2 dielets: under Poisson yield a 3x higher defect density still yields >90%, so the line can run looser particle control and fewer inline inspections; dielets are assembled by die-to-wafer hybrid bonding onto a logic base.
why: Cuts cleanroom-class and inspection capex (~10-15% of a fab) and lifts yield 20-30% on immature lines (Facts 4, 6).

title: Roll-to-roll memory foil laminated onto logic dies
idea: Run 10 um Invar foil through a newspaper-style web line: roll-to-roll sputter the IGZO/high-k/metal stack, pattern every gain-cell level in one pass with a multi-height self-aligned imprint (SAIL) stamp whose step heights encode each mask level, then laser-cut sheets and laminate them onto logic or base-die BEOL.
why: Capital intensity: a web line costs ~1/50 per m2 of a 300 mm fab and the multi-level stamp collapses ~5 masks into one imprint with zero inter-level overlay; density is relaxed (F 50-100 nm), so it targets a cheap capacity tier.

title: Embargo patterning: i-line stepper plus five spacer doublings
idea: A Soviet engineer denied scanners prints a 350 nm-pitch line grating on a 365 nm i-line stepper, then runs five self-aligned spacer-doubling loops (ALD oxide spacer, mandrel strip, repeat) to reach ~11 nm pitch, cutting lines with one coarse DUV trim mask; each loop needs only an ALD tool and an etcher.
why: Array line layers stop needing EUV or ArF immersion; i-line steppers cost ~$3-5M against ~$200M for EUV. Trades ~20 extra dep/etch steps per layer for ~60-80% less litho capex on those layers; accumulated line-edge roughness is the risk.

title: MLCC base-metal-electrode chemistry: nickel and acceptor-doped titanate capacitors
idea: The MLCC industry replaced Pd with Ni electrodes by firing BaTiO3 in reducing gas with Mn/Mg acceptor doping and a reoxidation anneal; apply the recipe to DRAM: Ni or TiN electrodes with Mg/Mn-doped SrTiO3 or CaTiO3 (thin-film k ~100-200), crystallized at low oxygen pressure and then reoxidized, with no Ru electrode and no Hf.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): meets the k ~70+ target, so AR can drop from ~70 to ~30-40, halving etch time and collapse risk; Sr, Ca, Ti, Mg, Mn, Ni, O are abundant.

title: Kagome basket weave: one grating reticle exposed at three angles
idea: Like triaxial kagome basketry, expose the same line/space grating reticle three times at 0, 60 and 120 degrees (wafer rotated in the pre-aligner between passes) into a hardmask stack that opens only where all three space sets overlap, yielding a hexagonal storage-node hole array from one mask.
why: Fact 4: one cheap, defect-tolerant grating replaces a contact-hole EUV mask; gratings print with the best resolution and depth of focus.

title: Aircraft-style leasing of fab tools across memory makers
idea: Magnify tool ownership to third-party lessors who buy EUV, etch and deposition tools and lease them, redeploying tools between memory makers as cycles shift, like aircraft leasing.
why: Capital intensity: moves $10B+ off the maker's balance sheet, raises tool utilization, and lowers the hurdle for a new US entrant.

title: Copy-exact university-toolset microfabs for low-capex capacity DRAM
idea: Box: business axis set to fab model. Build 5k-wafer/month 150-200 mm microfabs that copy a university nanofab toolset (used ALD, sputter, contact and imprint aligners, ICP, anodization) and run only university-buildable flows (anodic-pore capacitors, oxide TFTs, interference litho), sited by U.S. data centers to make CXL memory-expander tiers.
why: Capital: ~$50-100M per fab vs $15B and 1-2 years to build, diversifying supply; risk is the cost-per-bit gap to leading-edge DRAM (target within 2-3x for a capacity tier).

title: Dose-encoded single EUV exposure patterns two layers at once
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: expose wordline trenches at full dose and contact openings at half dose in one EUV pass on a dual-threshold resist stack; develop and etch the high-dose features first, then trim the resist to uncover the half-dose features for a second etch that is self-aligned by construction.
why: Removes one EUV exposure and one overlay error per merged pair; merging 2 of 5-7 EUV layers cuts EUV cost per wafer ~25-35% and tightens overlay (fact 4).

title: Bone-remodeling deposit-and-resorb supercycles self-align contacts without masks
idea: Bone is laid down and resorbed continuously, with net growth only where signals favor it; run ALD supercycles that deposit a dielectric everywhere and then a short etch that removes the thinner nuclei on metal but not the faster-grown film on oxide, repeated ~30x, so an isolation mask grows only on dielectric and contacts self-align.
why: Deletes 1-3 critical contact/via masks and their overlay budget (fact 4); est. 5-8% lower wafer cost.

title: Millisecond flash anneal crystallizes high-k after periphery is built
idea: TRIZ #21 Rushing through: a 1-3 ms xenon flash or laser anneal heats only the surface ZrO2/TiO2 dielectric above 900 C, forming high-k tetragonal/rutile phases (k ~45-80) while underlying periphery and metals stay below ~500 C.
why: Higher k holds Cs at ~half the aspect ratio, and the capacitor can be built last (after periphery or bonding), removing protective layers and steps (facts 1, 4, 10).

title: Industry-wide open cell-array mask standard shared by all makers
idea: Worse: every maker pays for proprietary array masks, and entrants must reinvent the cell. Flip: a consortium standardizes one array lattice and pitch and the masks/OPC for its critical array layers, licensed royalty-free. Vendors differentiate only in periphery, materials and capacitors.
why: Capital/entry barrier: entrants skip ~$1-2B of array integration R&D, and mask and OPC learning is pooled, enabling U.S. second sources.

title: MRAM's etch killer bypassed with ion-implant-defined magnetic junctions
idea: Everspin-era MRAM density and cost were throttled by etching magnetic stacks (non-volatile byproducts, sidewall redeposition, slow ion-beam etch). Deposit the MTJ stack blanket and define cells by implanting light ions (He+ or N+) through a hard mask to magnetically deaden the free layer between bits, leaving a planar, etch-free film.
why: Removes the ion-beam-etch throughput bottleneck and redeposition shorts; planar result is stackable; claims ~2-3x tool throughput and higher yield for DRAM-class-latency, unlimited-endurance cells.

title: Substitute hot DRAM capacity with hybrid-bonded stacks of depreciated 28 nm SRAM
idea: Stack 8-16 dies of high-density 28 nm SRAM from fully depreciated, non-EUV foundry lines directly on the accelerator by hybrid bonding as its hottest working-set tier, exploiting SRAM's non-destructive read and zero refresh.
why: Constraint: ~0.05-0.2 pJ/bit at um distance versus 3-15 pJ/bit for HBM/DDR5 (>10x); capital: no DRAM fab, no EUV. Cost per bit is ~10-20x worse, so it suits only the hottest few GB.

title: Counter-cyclical strategic DRAM reserve keeps fabs fully utilized
idea: Worse: let downturns idle fabs and freeze capex, so the next shortage is deeper. Flip: a government/hyperscaler reserve buys known-good DRAM wafers at a floor price during gluts, stores them in dry nitrogen vaults, and releases them during spikes, like a petroleum reserve for bits.
why: Capital intensity: guaranteed utilization lowers the risk premium on fab capex, keeps investment steady and damps 4x price swings.

title: Quorum-sensing wafer test: dies self-test and broadcast only anomalies
idea: Bacteria act only when a population signal crosses threshold; every die runs built-in self-test at wafer level, powered through one blanket probe membrane, and reports only pass/fail and compressed fail maps over a shared optical or RF channel, so the tester becomes a power supply plus listener instead of a pin-heavy ATE.
why: DRAM test and burn-in is ~10-15% of cost; est. 5x less tester capital per wafer and 3x shorter test time.

title: Mail sorting: NV array stores its own repair map, fuse-free
idea: Random stimulus 'mail sorting room' (routing table kept on site) -> because the cells are non-volatile, redundancy maps, trim codes and sense-amp offsets are written into reserved rows of the array itself. This eliminates the laser-fuse repair step, the e-fuse banks and their test-floor tools, and allows in-field re-repair.
why: Periphery (fact 7) shrinks ~2-4% of die area, laser repair tools leave the back-end, and test cost falls. Field self-repair raises effective yield.

title: Superlattice cleave-edge master stamps sub-20 nm DRAM lines
idea: Inverts 'line pitch comes from optics'. Grow a Si/SiGe or GaAs/AlGaAs superlattice by 1990s MBE, cleave and selectively etch its edge into a nanoimprint master whose line pitch equals layer thickness (~16-20 nm), then thermally imprint wordline/bitline gratings with a 1995-style imprint press, using a >=180 nm stepper only for coarse layers.
why: Sub-20 nm dense lines with zero EUV/ArF (fact 4); master replication makes a dense layer cost a few dollars.

title: Core-and-cavity casting: radial 3D DRAM from one hole mask
idea: Like sand casting where core prints define internal cavities, deposit a 40-tier stack on the periphery wafer, punch one mask of vertical bitline holes (larger openings on the same mask act as slits), and build each tier's ring IGZO transistor and coaxial capacitor by successive selective lateral recesses and ALD fills from that hole.
why: Facts 2 and 4: array patterning costs one critical mask regardless of tier count, giving a 3D NAND-like cost curve and ~4-8x bits per mask vs 2D.

title: Permanent-mold casting: reusable mold casts capacitor forests for transfer
idea: Instead of etching a fresh 60:1 mold on every wafer, make one ultra-precise AR>100 mold in single-crystal Si with an anti-stiction release liner, ALD-cast TiN/high-k/TiN shells in it, bond the filled mold to the transistor wafer's landing pads, release the capacitor forest, and reuse the mold ~100x like a die-casting die.
why: Facts 1 and 4: HAR etch and its masks amortize over ~100 wafers, so the mold can use slow, perfect processes; ~2x Cs from taller nodes without per-wafer HAR etch capex.

title: Self-unzipping resists recovered as monomer and repolymerized
idea: First principle: lithography needs only a transient chemical contrast, yet resist is burned or dumped. Use low-ceiling-temperature polymers (e.g., polyphthalaldehyde) that depolymerize fully to monomer under exposure or mild heat, capture the evaporated monomer in a cold trap on the track, then purify and repolymerize it.
why: Consumables and steps: removes solvent strip steps and resist waste; dry development also avoids pattern collapse.

title: Substitute tin-plasma EUV sources with one shared free-electron laser
idea: A single energy-recovery-linac FEL (~10 kW at 13.5 nm) is split to feed 10-20 scanners in a DRAM fab, replacing per-scanner laser-produced tin-plasma sources that waste >99% of their drive-laser power.
why: Fact 4: abundant dose allows cheaper, faster resists and higher throughput; source capex and power per wafer could fall ~3-5x. Single point of failure is the risk.

title: One free-electron laser feeds a whole fab of scanners
idea: Inverts 'every scanner carries its own plasma light source'. Build a ~10 kW energy-recovery-linac FEL in the fab basement and split its EUV beam to 8-12 source-less scanners.
why: The source is ~a third of scanner cost and the throughput limiter; ~3x power per scanner allows higher dose (fewer stochastics) or ~2x throughput (fact 4).

title: Free-electron-laser EUV source feeds a whole fab of scanners
idea: Ideal: EUV photons as cheap as DUV. Closest: one energy-recovery-linac free-electron laser produces multi-kW EUV, split by grazing-incidence optics to 10-20 scanners, replacing per-tool tin-droplet plasma sources.
why: Fact 4: source power limits throughput; ~3-5x power per scanner, no tin debris, lower energy per exposed wafer across a DRAM fab's EUV layers.

title: Fab in a tube: continuous vacuum track for capacitor module
idea: Po: the wafer never leaves the tool. Chain all ~40 capacitor-module steps (mold deposition, etch, clean, ALD, anneal) in a linear vacuum-linked track with single-wafer flow: no FOUPs, no queues, no air exposure between steps.
why: Cycle time and footprint: capacitor module from weeks to ~1 day, ~30% less WIP and floor area, fewer native-oxide cleans.

title: Trade lithography node for tier count: ArF-only 3D DRAM
idea: Shift density from the litho-bound x-y plane to the deposition-bound z axis: a horizontal-capacitor 3D DRAM drawn at F~38 nm with ArF single exposures only, reaching bit-density parity at ~120-150 Si/SiGe epitaxial tiers patterned by one high-AR slit plus staircase per block.
why: Zero EUV layers and ~40% fewer masks; deposition/etch passes cost ~5x less per wafer than EUV exposures, so capex per bit falls even with many tiers (Facts 2, 4).

title: Anodized-cookware pores: self-ordered alumina holes beyond 100:1
idea: Deposit 2 um of aluminium over the landing pads, pre-dimple it with the single added mask (10 nm-deep dot pattern), anodize in oxalic acid so pores nucleate at the dimples and grow straight down, open the barrier layer, and ALD the MIM capacitor into the pores.
why: Fact 1: a wet bath produces AR>100 holes at 30-60 nm pitch with no HAR plasma etch, for ~1.5-2x Cs; step capex down ~10x.

title: Heat-shrink film: relaxed-pitch mask halves pitch on release
idea: Like heat-shrink tubing, print the array at 2x pitch with the single added DUV mask onto a biaxially pre-strained polymer membrane on a carrier, release the strain so features shrink ~50% isotropically, then laminate the shrunken membrane onto the wafer as the etch hardmask.
why: Fact 4: relaxed-pitch printing on a cheap immersion mask replaces EUV or SAQP for one array layer; shrink uniformity across mats is the risk.

title: Turbine-blade EB-PVD columns: seeded columnar growth forms capacitor electrodes
idea: Borrow the electron-beam PVD that grows columnar thermal-barrier coatings on jet blades: place TiN seed dots with the single added mask, then evaporate TiN at grazing incidence with wafer rotation so self-shadowing grows isolated straight 1-2 um columns only on seeds, later coated with high-k and top plate.
why: Facts 1 and 4: high-AR electrodes by deposition with no mold or HAR etch; evaporators cost ~1/5 of HAR etch tools.

title: Stacked resonant-tunneling-diode latch replaces the storage capacitor
idea: Ideal: a cell that holds its state forever with one transistor. Closest: grow two series resonant-tunneling diodes (Si/SiGe or InGaAs/AlAs) as blanket epitaxy over the access-transistor contact (a Goto pair); their N-shaped I-V gives two stable storage-node voltages held by valley current, patterned with the same contact mask.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor and no refresh (saves ~46 fJ/bit and 10-20% bandwidth); one epi step replaces ~20 capacitor steps; needs peak-to-valley >10 at nA levels.

title: Metal SADP spacers become the finished bitlines
idea: Combine self-aligned double patterning with metallization: the spacer is deposited conformally as Ru or Mo rather than oxide, etched back, and the mandrel removed, so the spacers are the bitlines. Hard-mask transfer, metal deposition, metal etch and two cleans are skipped.
why: Removes ~8-10 steps per bitline layer and avoids stacking line-edge roughness from transfer etches; Ru/Mo also avoid tungsten (process steps, scarce resource).

title: Ni: nickel-seeded lateral crystallization of cheap amorphous tier stacks
idea: Deposit fast PECVD amorphous-Si/oxide stacks, open one vertical seed slit, add Ni there so NiSi2 fronts sweep laterally through every a-Si layer at ~550 C converting it to needle-like single-grain Si; the Ni-rich front ends in a sacrificial region that is cut away.
why: Fact 2: amorphous deposition is ~10x faster and cheaper than epitaxy and tolerates 100+ tiers; MILC gives near-crystalline mobility. Residual Ni leakage is the risk.

title: Ge: sacrificial germanium self-erases as GeO vapor
idea: Use pure Ge sacrificial layers in tier stacks; after the slit opens, lightly oxidize the exposed Ge and anneal at ~500-600 C so Ge + GeO2 -> 2GeO(g) volatilizes, propagating laterally and erasing the layer selective to Si and SiO2 with no etchant gas or liquid.
why: Fact 2 plus water: lateral sacrificial removal with no wet etch, rinse or stiction (~100% module water cut) in a batch furnace.

title: Plywood cross-lamination cancels warp in many-tier stacks
idea: Copy plywood's alternating grain: rotate each tier's line orientation (and its anisotropic film stress) 90 degrees relative to the tier below and alternate tensile/compressive liner recipes, so wafer bow cancels instead of accumulating through the stack.
why: Fact 2/yield: warp and overlay drift cap tier count; cancellation could allow ~2x more tiers before bow exceeds scanner and bonder chuck limits.
